newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn retreats from gold-grab after deputies baulk.
newsitem.headline: Bonn retreats from gold-grab after deputies baulk.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government retreated on Tuesday from a controversial plan to revalue central bank gold reserves after parliamentary deputies from Kohl's party baulked at the widely scorned operation.

Sources in Kohl's centre-right coalition said the government had abandoned its plans to reap billions of marks (dollars) in quick cash profits from the Bundesbank in 1997 and would instead accept the central bank's offer to transfer the funds in 1998.

The humbling retreat will make it harder for Germany to qualify for Europe's single currency because Bonn badly needed the 10 billion marks ($5.8 billion) from the gold and currency reserves to help it qualify.
The criteria agreed for membership of a single European currency pinpoint 1997 as the critical year for measuring government budget deficits to see who will qualify to join in 1999.

But the government's decision to back down amid withering criticism from the Bundesbank is likely to fortify Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) in the long run as the move is certain to restore public confidence in the euro.
"A solution is only possible with support of the Bundesbank," the coalition source told Reuters. "In face of the resistance from the Bundesbank, the revaluation for 1997 is no longer on the table."

Abandoning the plan to revalue the assets will mean that there is another 10 billion mark ($5.8 billion) hole in Bonn's 1997 budget, the official said. To fill that hole, the coalition is discussing privatisations, budget cuts and tax increases.

The agreement emerged after Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer met in Bonn for what was supposed to be a secret negotiation. Scores of journalists appeared at the Finance Ministry once word spread that Tietmeyer had arrived.

"We had good talks and we are on the way to an agreement," Waigel said. "We are indeed," Tietmeyer added, after the 30-minute long meeting. "I hope that we can come to an agreement." They declined to provide further details and walked quickly away.
Coalition sources confirmed Bonn was retreating moments later.

The central bank was not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insisted that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.

The government's unprecedented grab for the gold had stunned the Bundesbank and raised eyebrows throughout Europe, especially in countries where German officials had long been delivering stern lectures against such budgetary sleight-of-hand.

Parliamentary deputies had seemed surprised by the Bundesbank's firm rejection of the plan as many apparently assumed that Waigel had first won central bank backing. The fiercely independent Bundesbank enjoys wide respect in Germany and many deputies were clearly loath to take on the institution.
The Bundesbank sternly warned Bonn against resorting to tricks designed to squeeze Germany into Europe's currency union.

Angered by Waigel's plan to revalue reserves and use a part of those proceeds to fill budget holes this year, the Bundesbank compared Bonn's plans to practices of which Bonn itself had disapproved when proposed by other governments.
A CDU official said on Tuesday in Bonn that many conservative deputies objected to Waigel's plans to revalue against the central bank's will.

He added there were growing doubts in the CDU that the party could muster enough votes to pass Waigel's proposed law. The centre-right coalition has a slim 12-seat majority and several CDU and FDP deputies said they would not oppose the Bundesbank.

The beleaguered finance minister was even berated by leaders from his CSU party in Munich on Monday for resorting to budget tricks -- certainly a deflating experience for the man who normally enjoys solid backing in his own conservative party.
Michael Glos, head of the CSU parliamentary group, explained the retreat by saying that the differences between the Bundesbank and the government had been too small to fight over.
"A public dispute is not worth it either for the Bundesbank or for the government," he said. "We have a saying -- the smarter one backs down."
